d: 1. The reflux or flowing back of the tide; the return of the tidal wave toward the sea; -- opposed to flood; as, the boats will go out on the ebb. Thou shoreless flood which in thy ebb and flow Claspest the limits of morality! Shelley.

2. The state or time of passing away; a falling from a better to a worse state; low state or condition; decline; decay. Our ebb of life. Roscommon. Painting was then at its lowest ebb. Dryden. Ebb and flow, the alternate ebb and flood of the tide; often used figuratively. This alternation between unhealthy activity and depression, this ebb and flow of the in
w.e: AS. ebba; akin to Fries. ebba, D. eb, ebbe, Dan. & G. ebbe, Sw. ebb, cf. Goth. ibuks backward; prob. akin to E. even.

d: 1. To flow back; to return, as the water of a tide toward the ocean; -- opposed to flow. That Power who bids the ocean ebb and flow. Pope.
2. To return or fall back from a better to a worse state; to decline; to decay; to recede. The hours of life ebb fast. Blackmore.
w.e: AS. ebbian; akin to D. & G. ebben, Dan. ebbe. See 2d Ebb.

d: To cause to flow back. [Obs.] Ford.

a gradual decline (in size or strength or power or number)

d: 1. Consisting of ebony.
2. Like ebony, especially in color; black; dark. Night, sable goddess! from her ebon throne. Young.
Ebony. [Poetic] Framed of ebon and ivory. Sir W. Scott.
One who works in ebony.
To make black, or stain black, in imitation of ebony; as, to ebonize wood.

n: stain black to make it look like ebony

w.e: F. ébène, L. ebenus, fr. Gr. hobnim, pl. Cf. Ebon.

d: Made of ebony, or resembling ebony; black; as, an ebony countenance. This ebony bird beguiling my sad fancy into smiling. Poe.

d: Hebrew. [Obs.] Chaucer.

w.e: L. ebrietas, from. ebrius intoxicated: cf. F. ébriéte. Cf. So.

d: Addiction to drink; habitual drunkenness.
w.e: L. ebriositas, from ebriousus given to drinking, fr. ebrius. See Ebriety.

d: Inclined to drink to excess; intoxicated; tipsy. [R.] M. Collins.
To boil or bubble up. [Obs.] Prynne.
E*bullien*cy, n. “A boiling up or over; effervescence. Cudworth.”

n: overflowing with eager enjoyment or approval

d: E*bullien*cy, n. “A boiling up or over; effervescence. Cudworth.”
Boiling up or over; hence, manifesting exhilaration or excitement, as of feeling; effervescing. Ebullient with subtlety. De Quincey. The ebullient enthusiasm of the French. Carlyle.
w.e: L. ebulliens, -entis, p. pr. of ebullire to boil up, bubble up; e out, from + bullire to boil. See 1st Boil.

d: 1. A boiling or bubbling up of a liquid; the motion produced in a liquid by its rapid conversion into vapor.

2. Effervescence occasioned by fermentation or by any other process which causes the liberation of a gas or an aëriform fluid, as in the mixture of an acid with a carbonated alkali. [Formerly written bullition.]
3. A sudden burst or violent display; an outburst; as, an ebullition of anger or ill temper.
w.e: F. ébullition, L. ebullitio, fr. ebullire. See Ebullient.

d: A composition of dust of ivory or of bone with a cement; -- used for imitations of valuable stones and in making moldings, seals, etc. Knight.

w.e: L. eburnus of ivory, fr. ebur ivory: cf. F. éburnation. See Ivory.

n: a change that occurs in degenerative joint disease in which bone is converted into a dense smooth substance resembling ivory

d: Made of or relating to ivory.
w.e: L. eburneus, fr. ebur ivory. See Ivory.

d: The conversion of certain substances into others which have the appearance or characteristics of ivory.
w.e: L. eburnus of ivory (fr. ebur ivory) + facere to make.

d: Of or pertaining to ivory. [She] read from tablet eburnine. Sir W. Scott.
